p: A developer types on a laptop showing code, an adjacent smartphone screen activates displaying a colorful app, and an end card displays 'artifactshare.com — one live URL'.
A tool that lets developers easily deploy code or agent builds to a live mobile URL.

[{"timestamp":"00:00","observation":"Headline text overlaid as developer types on IDE."},{"timestamp":"00:04","observation":"Camera pans right to reveal phone turning on and loading preview."},{"timestamp":"00:06","observation":"CTA text overlays final shot with clean URL display."}]

The video effectively conveys the workflow from code to mobile preview within a tight duration. Audio cues and keystrokes line up reasonably well with visual transitions. Visual clarity remains solid throughout without noticeable generation defects.

           (creative_id, harness_version, hook_score, product_clarity, message_clarity,
            product_salience, cta_intent, visual_quality, artifact_score, overall_score,
            disqualified, failure_modes, critic_notes)
         values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
p: ["never shows an actual shared URL, browser, or live artifact page","phone screen only shows a generic abstract logo, not the product experience","code editor menu/labels render as garbled non-word text across 3 frames","no depiction of comments or teammate interaction promised by the message"]

The headline copy carries the message, but the visuals never deliver on it: we see a coder typing in a dark, code-editor-with-gibberish-labels scene, then a phone showing only an abstract two-shape logo screen — no browser, no URL bar, no artifact content, no comments. For a product whose entire pitch is 'one live URL your teammate opens,' failing to show a URL or a webpage undercuts product_clarity and salience badly. The final text card is crisp and the CTA URL is legible, which saves cta_intent, but this reads as generic 'developer at night' stock footage with a tagline slapped on rather than a real product demo.

p: Two colleagues sit next to each other viewing the same interface across a laptop and a tablet. A user taps the tablet to leave a comment pin, which simultaneously appears on the laptop, followed by an automated AI update that refreshes the page design live on both screens. The video concludes with a call-to-action slide.
You can leave comments directly on an artifact URL and have AI automatically update the live page without resharing links.

[{"timestamp":"00:00.800","observation":"Hand interacts with the tablet screen to place a comment pin."},{"timestamp":"00:01.800","observation":"Comment appears synchronized on both laptop and tablet displays."},{"timestamp":"00:04.600","observation":"A ripple effect indicates the AI refresh on the laptop interface, propagating across both screens."},{"timestamp":"00:06.400","observation":"Final CTA end card displays artifactshare.com."}]

The spot clearly communicates the core value proposition of live URL updates based on comments. Visual effects like the AI refresh ripple are effective, though motion tracking on screens feels slightly synthetic. Sound effects align cleanly with screen events.

p: ["headline text cropped at both screen edges in every hook frame","generic business-dashboard mockup, no code/terminal/dev cues for the target audience","comment represented by an ambiguous map-pin icon, not a recognizable comment/chat glyph","weak, unbranded product identity until the end card"]

The synced laptop/tablet split-screen does communicate 'same page updates live' when the mockup shifts from gray to blue after the pin-bubble appears, but the concept relies entirely on an abstract UI mock rather than anything resembling an AI-generated artifact or code output, so developers scrolling X have little reason to self-identify with the product. The hook line is cut off at both left and right margins throughout, hurting legibility exactly when it needs to land fastest. CTA card at the end is clean and unambiguous, which salvages some intent value.
